topic.title: Insurance bought for tax, not hospitals
topic.claim: Most of us buy health insurance in March for the tax form, which is why we find the room-rent clause in a hospital corridor.
topic.moment: An HR email reminding you to submit tax proofs, and a policy bought in 20 minutes.

turn.believed: Having a policy means you're covered.
turn.actually: A room-rent cap can cut the whole bill in proportion, so the cover shrinks right when you need it.

topic.feeling: Responsible on paper, exposed in real life.
topic.villain: Policies sold as tax savers with limits buried in fine print
topic.because: Tax season pushes people to buy fast and buy cheap. Cheap policies often save money through caps that only show up at claim time.
topic.payoff: Open your policy tonight and search one word: 'room'. That line decides your next hospital bill.
topic.behaviour: Salaried people buy policies before tax deadlines on price alone and never read sub-limits.
topic.mechanism: A deadline makes people buy the cheapest policy, and caps keep that policy cheap.
topic.group: Salaried earners and those buying cover for parents
topic.send_to: The sibling who bought parents' insurance in a rush last March.
topic.why_now: Renewals and tax planning both start creeping in before year-end.
topic.needs_facts: How proportionate deduction works when a room-rent limit is exceeded.

sources.fact: Reporting on General Insurance Council data calls March typically a strong month for health insurers, and retail health premiums grew 19% to about ₹48,952 crore by February 2026. It does not say that salaried buyers pick plans on price alone or skip sub-limits.
sources.excerpt: Premiums are expected to rise further in March, typically a strong month for insurers. Health premiums for April 2025 to February 2026 reached ₹1.24 lakh crore, already above the ₹1.18 lakh crore for all of FY25. Retail health premiums rose 19% to ₹48,952.01 crore, helped by the GST exemption on individual policies effective September 22, 2025.

sources.fact: If a policy caps room rent and the patient takes a costlier room, the insurer can pay less on the room and on related charges through proportionate deduction. This depends on the policy's terms and does not apply to every policy.
sources.excerpt: Some policies restrict the amount that can be claimed towards hospital room charges. In some policies, proportionate deductions can also apply to several related hospital expenses. Under the article's example, a Rs 5,000 limit against a Rs 10,000 room makes only half the room cost eligible. Where proportionate deduction applies, the insurer may similarly restrict certain associated expenses subject to the policy's terms.

sources.fact: IRDAI found that some insurers deducted amounts not admissible under policy terms, such as limiting room rent beyond those terms. This shows that room-rent disputes are not only a buyer's failure to read the policy.
sources.excerpt: IRDAI has pulled up eight major health insurers after finding serious lapses in how they handle claims. Even when claims were approved, some insurers were deducting amounts that were not admissible under the policy. For example, removing certain hospital charges or limiting room rent beyond policy terms. Essentially, policyholders weren't getting the full benefits they were entitled to.

cover.headline: We buy health insurance for [the tax form], not the hospital.
cover.sub: Which is why the fine print shows up at the billing desk.

paragraphs: We buy health insurance for the tax form, not the hospital.
slides.why_swipe: Why would a policy you paid for fail you?

paragraphs: HR sends the reminder: submit your investment proofs by Friday. You open a comparison site, sort by premium, low to high. Cheapest first.
slides.why_swipe: How long does buying it actually take?

paragraphs: Twenty minutes, one OTP, one PDF. If it's for your parents, the call home is "ho gaya, tension mat lo."
The PDF goes to the family WhatsApp group. Two thumbs up.
slides.why_swipe: What's inside the PDF that got two thumbs up?

paragraphs: Say your policy caps room rent at ₹5,000 a day. Your father gets a ₹10,000 room, the only one free.
The desk smells of phenyl. A stapler clicks through the file. Only half that room cost is eligible.
Your mother asks, "insurance toh hai na?" Half a room. Same illness.
slides.why_swipe: Is it only the room that gets cut?

paragraphs: But the cut doesn't always stay in the room. In some policies, several related charges on the bill can be reduced in the same proportion.
slides.why_swipe: So why did nobody catch this when buying?

paragraphs: The comparison site sorts by premium. The room cap isn't in that number. It sits in the policy wording, a few pages in.
And the premium you sorted for is low partly because of limits like that cap. The cheapest policy is cheap for a reason.
slides.why_swipe: So is the fine print the only problem?

paragraphs: Here's the uglier part. The system lets you down at both ends. The policy is sold fast, and the claim can be cut hard.
IRDAI found some insurers limiting room rent beyond what the policy allowed. So even a policy you've read can get cut.
slides.why_swipe: So who actually reads that line?

paragraphs: For the taxman, the premium receipt is enough.
The hospital billing desk only cares about one word inside the policy: room.

end.save: Read it again before you renew, and before HR's tax proof email lands.
end.send: Send to the sibling who bought your parents' insurance in a rush last March.

draft.caption: When did you last open your health policy, and was it for HR or for a hospital?
draft.alt_text: An eight-slide text post arguing that many Indians buy health insurance in a hurry for the tax form, sorted by lowest premium and forwarded to the family WhatsApp group, and only discover room-rent caps at the hospital. In a typical scene at the hospital desk, a ₹5,000 room cap against a ₹10,000 room makes only half the room cost eligible, while a mother asks if there isn't insurance. It explains that some policies cut related charges in the same proportion, that the cheapest premium is low partly because of caps like this, and that IRDAI found some insurers limiting room rent beyond policy terms, so even a read policy can get cut. It ends by saying the taxman only needs the premium receipt, while the hospital billing desk cares about one word in the policy: room.

claims.text: If a policy caps room rent at ₹5,000 a day and the room costs ₹10,000, only half the room cost is eligible.
In some policies, proportionate deduction can also cut several related hospital charges.
IRDAI found some insurers limiting room rent beyond policy terms.
For the tax deduction, the premium receipt is enough, regardless of what the policy covers.
